La documentación de esta integración la escribe su autor y, por ahora, solo está disponible en inglés.

Brings into Gladys the RGB lighting of a computer driven by
[OpenRGB](https://openrgb.org) (motherboard, RAM, graphics card, fans, LED
strips, keyboard, mouse…), through the **SDK server** of OpenRGB on your
local network: no account, no cloud.

> Never tested with a real device: built from the protocol of the OpenRGB SDK
> server (as the openrgb-sdk library reads it). Tell us on the forum how it
> goes. Not affiliated with OpenRGB.

## What you get

One device per controller OpenRGB sees, with:

- **Light**: on / off. Off sets every LED to black in the direct mode; on
  brings back the last color seen on (white if none);
- **Color**: every LED of the controller to that color, in the direct mode;
- **Effect mode**: the active mode (Direct, Static, Rainbow…), shown; changing
  it needs the option **Allow the effect modes**.

And, when OpenRGB has saved profiles, an **OpenRGB profiles** device: choosing
a profile loads it (every device at once), only with the option **Allow
loading the profiles**. OpenRGB does not tell which profile is active: the
list shows no read value.

No feature is a switch. The lights obey "turn off the lights" like any other.

Not handled: brightness, colors per LED or per zone, speed and direction of
the effects, resizing zones. The integration never sends a save request (no
mode saved to a device, no profile created or deleted); some devices keep
their last mode on their own.

Left out (the status says so): a controller without a "per-LED color" mode (it
can be neither colored nor turned off this way), and two identical
controllers without a serial at the same location (never a write on the wrong
one).

## Setup

1. In OpenRGB, **SDK Server** tab, click **Start Server** (or run
   `openrgb --server`, with `--server-port` if needed). Tick the automatic
   start if OpenRGB starts with the computer.
2. Give that computer a fixed address in your router.
3. In **Address of the OpenRGB computer**, type its IP address (or name), with
   `:port` only if not 6742.
4. Save, then add the devices from the **Discover** tab.

The SDK server has no password: any device on your network can drive it. Keep
it on a trusted network, never open it to the Internet.

The status tells how many controllers were read, those left out, a server that
does not answer (and when it is tried again), a service that answers but not
as OpenRGB.

**Test the connection** reads the server, or shows the last read when it is
younger than an interval (never faster than the interval).

## Which controller a device drives

OpenRGB numbers its controllers, but the number changes when it detects them
again. A device is therefore tied to its controller by a fingerprint of the
vendor, the name and the serial (or, without a serial, of the location OpenRGB
shows: bus and address). Before every write, the controller is read at its
number; if it is not that one anymore, the whole list is read to find it; if
it is gone: "nothing sent". A read serves the writes that follow on the same
connection until the next periodic read (plus 5 s), as long as OpenRGB does not
say its list changed: a scene on several controllers leaves without one read
per controller. Commands go one after the other (never interleaved); right
after a list change, on a slow server, the last ones of a scene may answer
"nothing sent" (Offs go one after the other and are kept). "On" always reads
the state before deciding: a scene turning several controllers on with a slow
server may set only some of them, even without a list change (measured: 3, 2
or 1 of 5 with answers in 300, 500 or 900 ms; the others answer "nothing
sent"). Space these actions in the scene (a wait of one to two seconds
between two "on").

If OpenRGB reorders its controllers without saying so, a command may reach,
until the next read, the controller that took the place: an Off may thus turn
a neighbor off. It is then not announced done: it is kept, and the next read
(or a new click) turns the right controller off; the neighbor stays off until
you turn it back on.

A USB device without a serial plugged into another port may thus show up as a
new device in Discover.

## Turning off

Off needs no option. It goes before the other commands and before the reads
(a read stuck for 1 s is cut), and cancels the commands of that controller
still waiting: nothing asked before the Off leaves after it. It also works
before the configuration is read (the address kept in `/data` serves).

When the read that follows does not show the controller off, the Off is kept
(in `/data`) and sent again by the next reads, 3 times at most. A newer
command that left for that controller (on, color, mode) or a profile asked
after the Off and loaded stops these resends. A profile asked before an Off
never leaves after it. At a start, a kept Off is sent again only when it is
less than 10 minutes old.

An Off is refused only when the controller is no longer on the server (or is
there twice, without a serial). When
the server does not answer, it is kept and sent at the next reads (3 times at
most).

## Answers to a command

- "Done": the read that follows shows the value asked;
- "Sent, without confirmation": it left, but the read does not show it (yet);
- "Nothing sent": refused before anything left (option off, controller not
  found, value not valid, an Off came after it, server unreachable).

## Data kept

In `/data`: the address of the server, the time of the last read (a restart
never reads sooner than the interval), for each controller its number in
OpenRGB and its last color on, the Offs to send again. No name, no serial.

## Parámetros de configuración

Estos son los parámetros que OpenRGB te pide en su pantalla de configuración en Gladys.

| Parámetro | Tipo | Obligatorio | Descripción |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Your OpenRGB server | `section` | No | Brings into Gladys the RGB devices OpenRGB drives on a computer (motherboard, RAM, graphics card, fans, LED strips, keyboard, mouse…), through the SDK server of OpenRGB on your network: each one becomes a light (on / off, color) with its effect mode. Start the SDK server in OpenRGB (SDK Server tab, or openrgb --server). It has no password: anyone on your network can drive it, keep it on a trusted network. Turning off needs no option and goes first. Effect modes and profiles change only once you allow them below. The integration never asks a device to save its settings (some keep their last mode on their own). Never tested with a real device: tell us on the forum how it goes. Not affiliated with OpenRGB. |
| Address of the OpenRGB computer | `string` | Sí | The IP address (or name) of the computer running OpenRGB, with :port only if the SDK server does not listen on 6742. Give that computer a fixed address in your router. |
| Read every (seconds) | `number` | No | How often the devices are read: 10 s by default, 5 s at least. |
| Allow the effect modes | `boolean` | No | Lets Gladys switch a device to another of its effect modes (rainbow, breathing…). Off by default: the mode is shown, not changed. |
| Allow loading the profiles | `boolean` | No | Lets Gladys load a profile saved in OpenRGB (it sets every device at once). Off by default. Profiles are never saved nor deleted. |
| Language of the names | `select` | No | Used for the names of the features added from now on. |

## Cómo instalar OpenRGB en Gladys

1. En Gladys, abre **Integraciones**: OpenRGB aparece en el catálogo junto a las integraciones nativas, con una insignia de comunidad.
2. Haz clic en **Instalar**. Gladys descarga la imagen Docker (`ghcr.io/lm1lc3n7/gladys-openrgb:0.1.1`), la ejecuta en un entorno aislado del núcleo y genera la interfaz de la integración (dispositivos, descubrimiento y configuración).
3. Abre la pantalla de **Configuración** de la integración, rellena los parámetros y guarda.
4. También puedes instalarla directamente desde la URL de su repositorio: [https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-openrgb](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-openrgb).

OpenRGB requiere Gladys `>=5.1.0`. El catálogo de Gladys se actualiza cada hora, así que una nueva versión está disponible como máximo una hora después de publicarse.

¿Todavía no usas Gladys? Es gratuito y de código abierto: [sigue la guía de instalación](/es/docs/) para empezar.

## Sobre las integraciones externas

OpenRGB es una **integración externa**: una integración comunitaria empaquetada como contenedor Docker y publicada en GitHub. Gladys la instala con un clic y la ejecuta en un entorno aislado del núcleo. La publica y mantiene [LM1LC3N7](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7), no el equipo principal de Gladys.
